stories.headline: A ‘one-man’ Election Commission? Inside the allegations against CEC Gyanesh Kumar
stories.title: A ‘one-man’ Election Commission? Inside the allegations against CEC Gyanesh Kumar
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: On October 6, around 240 Opposition MPs marched towards the Election Commission of India’s office in New Delhi, demanding a meeting with Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and seeking his resignation.
They were stopped a few hundred metres from the Commission’s office and eventually sat in protest.
The Election Commission, however, gave a different account.
In a press note issued that evening, it said it learnt through the media that MPs wanted to meet the Commission and that, until 4 pm, no political party representative had sought an appointment.
Later, Delhi Police informed the Commission that a delegation led by Leader of Opposition Rahul Gandhi wanted to submit a memorandum.
The ECI said the delegation wanted to meet at Parliament House Annexe, whereas its protocol required such meetings to be held at the Commission’s premises.
It offered to send a senior-most officer to receive the memorandum, but the MPs declined.
The explanation may address the question of procedure.

But it does not answer a larger question that has been building around Gyanesh Kumar for more than a year — how does the Chief Election Commissioner deal with political parties that question him and how does he deal with the two Election Commissioners who sit alongside him?
The October 6 incident is only the latest in a series of episodes involving the CEC and Opposition parties.
Once, Kumar publicly demanded that Rahul Gandhi either substantiate his allegations against the Election Commission through an affidavit or apologise to the nation.
In yet another, a political delegation claimed that Kumar asked them to “get lost” within minutes of their meeting.

stories.headline: World has not forgotten 9/11, 26/11, Pahalgam attacks: India at UN
stories.title: World has not forgotten 9/11, 26/11, Pahalgam attacks: India at UN
stories.summary: United Nations, Oct 8: Exposing Pakistan’s doublespeak on terrorism at the UN, India has called out Islamabad’s efforts to gloss over its state support for terror by announcing rewards for JeM chief Masood Azahar, underlining that the world has not forgotten 9/11, 26/11 and Pahalgam attacks. India on Wednesday exercised its Right of Reply in response to the Pakistan representative’s statement in the Sixth Committee of the UN General Assembly on the Agenda Item: Measures to Eliminate International Terrorism. “Pakistan speaks of combating terrorism while seeking to obscure the very question that this committee must confront: What happens when terrorists are financed, facilitated, trained, sheltered, or supported from the territory of a state?” First Secretary in the Permanent Mission of India to the UN Raghoo Puri said. He said India has been consistent on this question, underscoring that terrorism cannot be defeated by declarations and instead requires action against its perpetrators, organisers, financiers, and sponsors. “For years, Pakistan has presented itself as a frontline state in combating terrorism and as a victim while masking the fact that the Frankensteins the Pakistani state has created and lost control over have moved from wreaking havoc in neighbouring countries to doing the same in Pakistan,” Puri said. Calling out Pakistan’s doublespeak on terrorism, Puri said the country “glosses over its state support for terrorism by announcing enhanced rewards for apprehending UN-listed head of Jaish-e-Mohammed terrorist and mastermind of several attacks against my country, Masood Azhar.” He said the world is aware of Pakistan’s financial support to terrorism. “Yet, we also remember that just a few months ago, Pakistani representatives used this forum to call the Jaish-e-Mohammed a defunct organisation. The world has seen the script play earlier, and we are clear-eyed that this time also it is going to be no different,” he said. Puri said that when the media can reach Azhar and get confirmation from him about the success of Operation Sindoor, “surely the Pakistani state knows his whereabouts”. In May last year, India had launched Operation Sindoor targeting terror infrastructure in Pakistan and Pakistan-occupied Kashmir in retaliation for the dastardly April 22 terror attack in Pahalgam in Jammu and Kashmir perpetrated by The Resistance Front, a proxy of Pakistan-based terror group Lashkar-e-Taiba, in which 26 civilians, mostly tourists were killed. ExploreHistory Earlier this month, India had dismissed as “gimmicks” Pakistan’s fresh announcement of a bounty of seven million rupees on Azhar, demanding that Islamabad take “concrete action” to combat terrorism. India has for years accused Pakistan of sheltering Azhar, while Pakistan has maintained that he fled to Afghanistan – a claim rejected by Afghanistan’s Taliban government. For the last few years, Islamabad has claimed that the JeM founder has been operating from Afghanistan. However, the Taliban regime dismissed Pakistan’s repeated claims, with a senior Afghan Foreign Ministry official saying he is not in the country. Islamabad’s fresh announcement on the reward for information on Azhar came as it faces pressure from the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) to crack down on terror groups and their leadership. The Paris-based global watchdog is set to review Pakistan’s anti-terrorism efforts at its upcoming plenary. Pakistan was placed under the FATF grey list between 2018 and 2022 for its systemic deficiencies in anti-money laundering and its failure to counter-terror financing. Puri also recalled a recent statement by Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz, daughter of former Pakistan prime minister Nawaz Sharif, who had said,“The unfortunate thing is that the threat [Punjab] faces comes less from my neighbouring countries and more from my neighbouring provinces.” Exposing this “dark secret”, Puri said, “You cannot run with the hares and hunt with the hounds. Reality never works like that.” “When terrorist groups are allowed to operate under state political power, international commitments become meaningless and when perpetrators are provided safe havens, the victims of terrorism are denied justice,” he said. “The world has not forgotten 9/11 and where its perpetrators, including Osama bin Laden, were caught. The world has not forgotten 26/11. The world has not forgotten Pahalgam,” Puri said, adding that the list, “unfortunately”, is painfully long. “The victims in Pahalgam were not asked about their political orientation, they were asked about their religion. It is therefore deeply ironic that Pakistan speaks of combating religious hatred while allowing the conditions that enable it to persist and thrive, especially by fomenting cross-border terrorism,” he said. “Pakistan continues with its narrative building, misinformation, and disinformation. If bombed-out airfields and cratered runways look like victory to Pakistan, they are of course welcome to enjoy it,” Puri said. “Any regime against terrorism to be effective must do two things: assign responsibility and ensure accountability. India will defend its people, and continued terrorism against India will have consequences,” he added. In another Right of Reply, Puri said India rejected Pakistan’s “circular economy” of words and narratives. “If this much effort had actually been made in countering terrorism rather than narrative building, misinformation, and disinformation, the world would have been a better place. But nothing more can be expected from a Form 47 government,” he said, referring to a term used to describe allegations of rigging and manipulation in Pakistan’s 2024 general elections.

stories.headline: Zero tolerance towards terrorism biggest takeaway of Modi Govt: R S Pathania
stories.title: Zero tolerance towards terrorism biggest takeaway of Modi Govt: R S Pathania
stories.summary: Jammu, Oct 8: “Zero tolerance towards terrorism in all its forms has been one of the biggest takeaways of the Modi government,” said BJP MLA Udhampur East Ranbir Singh Pathania, while addressing the gathering following a Rangoli competition organised at Ayesha International School, Udhampur. Pathania said that under the decisive leadership of Prime Minister Narendra Modi, a new sense of security and confidence has been created in Jammu and Kashmir. He said that the government has taken firm and uncompromising measures against terrorism, its financing and its support ecosystem. “Hawala funding has been curbed; the terror ecosystem has been dismantled and those providing shelter and support to terrorism have also faced decisive action. The message is loud and clear — the central government has zero tolerance towards terrorism,” BJP MLA said. He said that the demolition and attachment of properties associated with terrorists and their supporters also sent a strong signal that the government would not allow the support infrastructure of terrorism to flourish. “PM Modi’s journey is a story of leadership during crises,” said Pathania. Referring to the 25 years of public service of Narendra Modi, he said that his journey has been marked by leadership during some of the most challenging phases faced by the country. He recalled the challenges posed by the COVID-19 pandemic, economic disruptions, demonetisation, geopolitical developments, Central Asian challenges and evolving global circumstances, saying that India emerged from these difficult phases with greater confidence and a stronger global standing. Pathania said that the Prime Minister's clarion call of “Viksit Bharat” and the vision of making India one of the world's top three economies has provided the nation with a clear developmental direction. He said, “PM’s “We will do it” - is not merely a slogan; it is an inspirational vision and an undertaking for every citizen. The journey towards Viksit Bharat has to become a people's movement.” Speaking about development in Udhampur East, Pathania said that road connectivity remained one of his foremost priorities. He kick-started road works from Ambi Nallah towards Spa village, Sundla, as well as the main road leading to Shri Sahib Bandagi Ashram at Nakki, despite challenging weather conditions. “Roads are the arteries of a nation. Better connectivity means better access to education, healthcare, markets, tourism and employment. I am determined to make Udhampur East a hub of robust road connectivity.” Pathania said. He further announced that the Dhar Road would be fully macadamised shortly, while potholes and damaged stretches would also be attended to through necessary patchwork and repair works. Pathania said that the focus would remain on durable and quality infrastructure rather than temporary interventions, adding that improved connectivity would give a major boost to the rural economy, tourism and movement of people. He said that the vision of Viksit Bharat has to begin from the grassroots, with developed villages, better roads, stronger infrastructure and improved public facilities. The MLA also interacted with students and participants during the Rangoli competition and appreciated their creativity and enthusiasm.

stories.headline: The Genius of Bharat
stories.title: The Genius of Bharat
stories.summary: Diversity, by itself, does not produce unity. A society may contain many languages, religions, customs and communities without granting them equal dignity or a meaningful place in common public life. Diversity becomes pluralism only when difference is accepted as legitimate, when communities encounter one another without seeking to erase one another, and when citizens recognise that their distinct identities can coexist within a shared national framework. That transformation requires more than cultural tolerance. It requires fraternity—the civic willingness to regard those who are different as fellow members of the same political community. And fraternity requires constitutionalism: the discipline that places every citizen, community and government under the authority of equal rights, lawful institutions and accountable public power. India’s diversity is visible everywhere—in its languages, religions, philosophies, customs, cuisines, dress, literature, music and regional traditions. But beneath this extraordinary variety lies a long, though uneven, history of accommodating difference. The Indian achievement is not that conflict or exclusion disappeared. It is that the subcontinent repeatedly generated cultural practices, intellectual traditions and political arrangements through which difference could be negotiated rather than permanently converted into separation. That is the foundation on which Indian pluralism must be understood. Diversity is a fact. Pluralism is a philosophy. Fraternity is its civic ethic. Constitutionalism is the rule that makes it durable. A diverse society may simply contain many communities. A plural society develops the ethical and institutional capacity to allow those communities to coexist with dignity, engage with one another and contribute to a common public life. India’s achievement has often been to turn diversity into a civilisational resource, although this achievement has never been complete or free from conflict. For thousands of years, the subcontinent has been a site of intellectual disagreement. Its philosophical traditions did not develop around a single universally authorised doctrine. Vedic and Upanishadic texts explored questions about existence, the self and ultimate reality. Buddhism and Jainism challenged established assumptions and developed influential alternative traditions. The schools commonly classified as Vedanta, Samkhya, Yoga, Nyaya and Mimamsa, among others, developed distinct arguments and often debated one another. The Buddhist emperor Ashoka gave one expression to this principle in his edicts. In the 12th Rock Edict, generally dated to the third century BCE, he urged people not to disparage other sects and argued that honouring one’s own tradition should not involve denigrating others’. His message was not that all beliefs were identical. It was an appeal for restraint, learning and mutual respect in a religiously diverse society. The edict should be understood as evidence of an imperial ethical and political ideal, not as proof that all communities throughout the subcontinent practised equal tolerance. Yet disagreement itself became part of the intellectual culture. This is a significant feature of many Indian traditions. Truth was not always presented as something that could be exhausted by one formulation. The search for truth could proceed through dialogue, debate, experience and contemplation. The dialogues preserved in some Upanishads, Buddhist and Jain traditions of disputation, and the later debates associated with figures such as Adi Shankaracharya reflect the importance accorded to argument. They do not, however, prove that Indian society was uniformly tolerant or free from hierarchy and exclusion. Intellectual openness and social inequality often coexisted. That intellectual pluralism also found expression in India’s literary and cultural traditions. The Ramayana and Mahabharata travelled across the subcontinent, acquiring regional languages, interpretations and artistic forms. Kamban’s Tamil Ramavataram, Tulsidas’s Awadhi Ramcharitmanas and Krittibasi’s Bengali Ramayana are among the best-known examples of retelling. The many versions found across South and Southeast Asia demonstrate how a shared narrative could be adopted without being reproduced identically. Sanskrit interacted with Tamil, Prakrit, Pali and later with India’s many regional languages. Local traditions absorbed wider civilisational themes while retaining their distinctive character. The result was not cultural uniformity. It was a form of cultural federation. India’s diversity is therefore not merely the consequence of geography. It is also the product of centuries of migration, exchange, adaptation and political change. Kashmir provides a particularly important example. The Valley became a major centre of Sanskrit learning, philosophy, aesthetics and spiritual inquiry. Kashmir Shaivism is associated with thinkers such as Vasugupta, Utpaladeva and Abhinavagupta. Abhinavagupta’s writings on aesthetics, including his interpretation of rasa, influenced later Indian thinking about drama and artistic experience. Lal Ded’s verses have been read across religious boundaries, while the teachings associated with Sheikh Noor-ud-din Noorani, or Nund Rishi, became an important part of Kashmir’s spiritual heritage. The term Kashmiriyat is often used to describe an ideal of shared Kashmiri belonging across religious communities. Its meaning and historical application are debated, and the region’s history includes periods of coexistence as well as conflict, displacement and political violence. Nevertheless, the ideal reflects an aspiration toward a common civic and cultural identity. It should not be presented as an uncontested description of all periods of Kashmiri history. The larger lesson is important. Civilisations can become richer when communities do not merely coexist but encounter one another. Indian pluralism has also been shaped by communities that arrived from outside the subcontinent. Jewish communities established settlements in places including Kerala and Maharashtra, preserving their religious traditions while participating in local society. The Bene Israel community in the Konkan region and the Cochin Jews in Kerala are examples of communities that made India their home over many centuries. Parsis, members of the Zoroastrian faith, migrated to western India from Iran over successive periods, particularly after the Arab conquest of Persia, although the precise chronology and scale of these migrations are matters of historical study. A well-known Parsi tradition recounts that a local ruler symbolised the limits of his kingdom with a vessel filled with milk, and that the Parsi leader responded by adding sugar to it, suggesting that the newcomers would blend into society while enriching it. The story is best treated as cultural memory rather than independently verified history. It nevertheless captures an important element of Parsi self-understanding. Parsis later made major contributions to India’s industrial, philanthropic and public life. The Tata family helped build important enterprises and supported scientific, educational and cultural institutions. Parsi figures such as Dadabhai Naoroji, the first Asian elected to the British House of Commons, played a significant role in public life and the freedom movement. Their history shows how a small community can preserve its identity while contributing substantially to a wider national project. Christianity also has a long history in India. The Saint Thomas Christian tradition in Kerala traces its origins to the early centuries of the Common Era, although the precise historical details of its earliest beginnings remain debated. Christian communities and institutions have contributed significantly to education, healthcare, printing and social reform. Institutions such as St. Xavier’s College in Mumbai and Christian Medical College in Vellore are prominent examples, alongside numerous schools, hospitals and charitable organisations serving people of many faiths. India’s Muslim communities have likewise shaped the country’s shared identity in countless ways. Urdu poetry, Hindustani music, qawwali, architecture, cuisine, crafts and scholarship are not external additions to Indian culture; they are part of its living inheritance. Bhakti and Sufi traditions sometimes created spaces of spiritual exchange, although the relationship between them varied across regions and periods. Figures such as Kabir, Guru Nanak, Khwaja Moinuddin Chishti and Amir Khusrau are remembered across community boundaries, even though their historical contexts and religious affiliations should not be collapsed into a single “syncretic” narrative. The cultural histories of Bengal, Punjab, the Deccan and Kashmir show how interaction produced new forms of language, music and devotion. The Indian experience demonstrates that national identity need not require cultural erasure. One can preserve one’s language and still be Indian. One can practise one’s faith and still be fully committed to the Republic. One can celebrate one’s regional heritage while embracing a larger national identity. This layered belonging is not a weakness. It is one of India’s greatest strengths. The Constitution gave this aspiration a modern democratic and legal framework. It did not simply codify an uninterrupted ancient tradition; it also responded to colonial rule, social inequality, Partition and the demands of a modern republic. The Preamble commits the Republic to justice, liberty, equality and fraternity. Fundamental Rights protect equality and several forms of individual and collective freedom. Article 14 guarantees equality before the law and equal protection of the laws. Article 15 prohibits discrimination by the State on specified grounds, including religion, race, caste, sex and place of birth, subject to constitutionally permitted affirmative-action provisions. Article 16 guarantees equality of opportunity in public employment, again subject to specified exceptions and reservations. Article 17 abolishes untouchability and makes its practice an offence. Article 25 protects freedom of conscience and the freedom to profess, practise and propagate religion, subject to public order, morality, health and the other provisions of Part III. article_sentences: In a major push toward digital integration and systemic efficiency in motor accident claim settlements, the Supreme Court has directed the Union government, States, Union Territories to mandatorily integrate key digital platforms, including the Electronic Detailed Accident Report (eDAR), VAHAN, SARATHI, and the Insurance Information Bureau (IIB), within four weeks to facilitate seamless sharing of accident-related information, vehicle and insurance records, and previous claim histories.
The directions have been passed in a case where the Court has been dealing with the issue of fake accident claims.
The integration must also extend to hit-and-run cases and the PM-RAHAT Scheme, enabling early accident alerts to be transmitted directly to insurers, the court said.

A bench of Justice Ahsanuddin Amanullah and Justice Prasanna B Varale granted a four-week time to the authorities to comply with the directive regarding the integration of the databases, while continuing hearing a case where it expanded a motor accident compensation dispute into a wider inquiry of suspected fraudulent insurance claims after allegations emerged that an insured vehicle had figured in multiple accident cases.

“…a direction is issued to all the concerned authorities, including the Union of India and States to ensure interlinking of VAHAN, SARATHI, eDAR and IIB for seamless cross- reference of accident reports, vehicle/insurer records and prior claim(s) history.
This integration shall extend to Hit-and-Run and PM-RAHAT Schemes, enabling early accident alerts directly to insurers.
The same be done within four weeks from today positively.

On the next, compliance report as also details with regard to the queries of the Court as indicated in the previous orders be brought on record by way of an affidavit by the parties concerned.”, observed the court.

The direction seeks to improve coordination between transport authorities, accident-reporting agencies and insurance institutions by enabling relevant information to be accessed across the interconnected platforms.
The Court also noted that, although the eDAR portal operated by the National Informatics Centre had been established, only a few States had started uploading data onto it.
Consequently, the Court directed all States to ensure that the relevant data was uploaded to eDAR without delay.

Apart from the directions concerning digital integration, the Court expressed serious concern over repeated failures by certain insurance companies to comply with its earlier directions regarding appearance before the Court.

article_sentences: New Delhi: The Supreme Court on Thursday directed the Centre to constitute a committee to examine the need for statutory regulation of pharmaceutical companies' marketing practices, including the offering of gifts, hospitality and other benefits to doctors to promote their products.

A Bench of Justices Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta passed the direction while hearing a plea seeking statutory regulation of pharmaceutical marketing practices and measures to curb unethical interactions between drug companies and doctors.

During the proceedings, Solicitor General Tushar Mehta had informed the Justice Nath-led Bench that the Union government would constitute a three-member committee to examine whether a statutory framework was required to regulate pharmaceutical companies and, if so, recommend the form such regulation should take.
The Centre submitted that the existing regulatory framework provides for disciplinary action against doctors who accept such benefits from pharmaceutical companies.
However, the issue of statutory regulation of pharmaceutical companies themselves would be examined by the proposed committee.
The committee will consider suggestions and objections received from stakeholders and make recommendations to the Centre on the need for statutory regulation of pharmaceutical marketing practices.

The proceedings arose from concerns over the practice of pharmaceutical companies offering freebies, gifts, hospitality, travel facilities or other benefits to doctors as incentives for prescribing their products.

The petitioner's side submitted that the existing framework created an asymmetry by providing for consequences for doctors who accepted such inducements while lacking a corresponding statutory mechanism to regulate or penalise pharmaceutical companies that offered them.
The Centre has been asked to file an affidavit regarding compliance with the Supreme Court's directions, and the matter will be taken up for further hearing on January 29.
The issue of pharmaceutical marketing practices has also come against the backdrop of the apex court examining wider concerns relating to medicine pricing and affordability.

In a separate set of PILs concerning the regulation of medicine prices, generic medicines, medical devices and prescription practices, the same Bench had questioned the wide disparity between the price at which medicines are supplied to retailers and their MRP.
In a previous hearing, the Supreme Court had questioned the Centre over a cancer medicine carrying an MRP of Rs 27,000 while being supplied to retailers for around Rs 2,700 to Rs 3,000.

stories.headline: Rethinking Progress: Plans, Policies and Projects
stories.title: Rethinking Progress: Plans, Policies and Projects
stories.summary: What does progress mean for Jammu and Kashmir? More roads? More tourists? More hotels and townships? More industrial investment? Higher horticultural production? More construction? All of these can contribute to economic development. Jammu and Kashmir unquestionably needs investment, jobs, higher household incomes, better infrastructure and improved public services. But recent events across the Himalayas increasingly compel us to ask a deeper question: Are the conventional ways in which we define, plan and measure development adequate for a fragile mountain region facing accelerating climatic and ecological change? Dr. R. Balasubramaniam, Member of NITI Aayog, raises precisely this question in his recent article, Rethinking Progress. Reflecting on the devastating August disaster in Nepal and other extreme events, he argues that such tragedies should not simply result in stronger bridges, better warning systems and more disaster-response infrastructure. They should make us examine the assumptions underlying the development model itself. His argument moves beyond conventional sustainability towards what he calls regenerative development: instead of asking only how development can do less environmental damage, we should ask how development can strengthen ecosystems, communities and infrastructure together so that the systems upon which society depends become more resilient rather than progressively depleted. For Jammu and Kashmir, this is an important and timely proposition. From more development to better progress The challenge before J&K is certainly not to choose between development and environmental protection. That is a false choice. The challenge is to ensure that economic development produces durable progress. A road that improves connectivity but greatly increases landslide or flood exposure cannot be judged only by kilometers constructed. Tourism that increases visitor numbers and revenues but overwhelms water supplies, mobility systems, waste infrastructure and fragile landscapes cannot be judged simply by arrivals. Urban expansion that creates valuable real estate while removing drainage channels, wetlands or flood-storage areas may increase today’s asset values while increasing tomorrow’s public liabilities. And agricultural intensification that raises production in the short term but depletes soils, water or ecosystem health may not ultimately increase farmer prosperity. Therefore, the question shifts from how much development are we achieving to what kind of progress is that development producing? That distinction should sit at the center of the next generation of planning in Jammu and Kashmir. Our problem is not the absence of plans J&K does not suffer from a shortage of plans, policies and projects. Tourism has policies and destination-development programs. Agriculture and horticulture have productivity strategies. Urban areas have master plans. Roads, industry, housing, water supply, flood management, forestry and conservation have their own programs and institutional machinery. Most address legitimate needs. The underlying weakness is different: we lack a sufficiently strong common ecological and spatial framework within which these sector plans are designed, reconciled and implemented. Government necessarily works departmentally. Landscapes do not. A forested slope may simultaneously regulate runoff, stabilize soil, store carbon, support biodiversity, provide livelihoods and influence downstream water security. A wetland may look like undeveloped land while performing valuable flood-storage and water-quality functions. Tourism generates employment and income but also generates traffic, water demand, wastewater, solid waste and land-use change. When institutions optimize these objectives independently, individually rational projects can collectively produce irrational outcomes. That is fundamentally a planning-architecture problem. Nature performs infrastructure functions. Forests moderate runoff and erosion. Wetlands absorb and store floodwater. Healthy watersheds protect downstream roads, settlements and reservoirs. Healthy soils store water and sustain agricultural productivity. Urban green systems reduce heat and improve human wellbeing. Balasubramaniam’s call for regenerative development and the Nature-based development planning approach, therefore, converge on an important idea: Progress should leave our economic, social and ecological systems stronger not weaker. For planning purposes, this means designing built and natural infrastructure as complementary parts of the same development system. So, where do we start? Start with the geography that actually connects us Government operates through districts, municipalities, departments and development authorities. Water does not. Floods follow topography. Sediment moves downstream. Forest degradation affects water flows. Urbanization alters runoff. Tourism pressures spill across administrative boundaries. For the Kashmir Valley, the Jhelum River Basin provides an obvious higher-level ecological planning framework. Snow and glaciers, upper catchment forests, springs, tributaries, agriculture, orchards, wetlands, floodplains, Srinagar and Wular are components of one interconnected hydrological system. This does not require another bureaucracy. It requires a nested planning architecture. At the highest level should be J&K’s strategic economic, social and resilience objectives. Basin and landscape planning should establish the underlying resource envelope: water availability, ecological assets, climate and disaster risks, natural infrastructure and broad carrying capacities. Sector strategies for tourism, horticulture, agriculture, forestry, urbanization, transport, industry and energy should then operate within that framework. These strategies should subsequently be differentiated across sub-basins, districts, towns and development-authority areas, while implementation remains with existing departments and agencies. Strategic Environmental Assessment (SEA) should become standard planning practice Changing the architecture also requires changing our assessment tools. Environmental Impact Assessment, or EIA, generally operates at the individual-project stage. By then, many important strategic decisions—location, development model, scale and investment direction—may already have been made. J&K should, therefore, introduce SEA, as standard good practice for major sector strategies, spatial plans and sub-basin development plans. The difference is significant. An EIA asks: What environmental impacts will this particular road create? An SEA asks: What mobility strategy should this region pursue? Where should new infrastructure go? What alternatives exist? What development will be induced by improved accessibility? And what are the combined consequences for communities, forests, water, climate resilience and disaster risk? Similarly, rather than assessing tourism projects one hotel at a time, an SEA of a destination or tourism strategy would examine its proposed scale and spatial pattern against water availability, waste-management capacity, mobility, ecosystem sensitivity and community needs. Consequently, SEA moves environmental thinking upstream, where fundamental development choices are still open. Look at cumulative impacts, not projects in isolation SEA - Cumulative Impact Assessment (CIA) are essential planning tools: A single hotel may appear acceptable. So might another. And another. But fifty individually acceptable developments can collectively overwhelm a destination’s roads, water supply, sewage system, waste infrastructure, landscapes and communities. The same applies to roads, hydropower, urban construction and industrial development. Therefore, our planning system needs to ask not merely what each project does, but what all foreseeable development together will do to a landscape or sub-basin. This brings carrying capacity to the center of planning: How much water is sustainably available? How much tourism can a destination accommodate? How much traffic can its road network absorb? How much waste can be treated? How much construction can occur without increasing flood risk? How will these thresholds change under global warming? These are not merely environmental questions. They are questions about the sustainability of economic assets and public investment. Geo-AI can make this practical We also possess capabilities that earlier generations of planners did not. GIS, remote sensing, digital elevation models, hydrological and climate modelling, sensors and artificial intelligence can combine information on forests, wetlands, rivers, glaciers, snow, orchards, settlements, infrastructure, tourism, pollution and hazards. A J&K Geo-AI-enabled planning platform could allow decision-makers to test alternative development scenarios before investments become locked in. What happens to runoff and flood risk? What additional water and energy will be required? What traffic and waste will be generated? Which natural assets will be lost? Which communities benefit and which assume additional risks? Could Nature-based Solutions reduce or complement expensive engineered infrastructure? Technology will not replace political judgement. But it can greatly improve the evidence upon which judgement is exercised. From sustainability towards regeneration J&K already has part of the institutional foundation for this approach. The Jammu and Kashmir Water Resources (Regulation and Management) Act, 2010 calls for planning on a hydrological-unit basis using multidisciplinary approaches and explicitly incorporates basin-master planning. The opportunity is to extend this principle into the wider development-planning architecture. Balasubramaniam’s argument adds another important dimension. Perhaps the objective should no longer be merely to make development less damaging. In particularly fragile landscapes, the ambition should progressively become regenerative: restoring watersheds, strengthening communities, improving soils, rebuilding ecological resilience, and making infrastructure safer while simultaneously expanding livelihoods and economic opportunities. So, what should progress mean for J&K? Jammu and Kashmir must seek economic growth and prosperity. But progress in a Himalayan region should mean more than increasing physical assets and economic transactions. It should mean higher household incomes and productive employment; resilient infrastructure; secure water supplies; healthy forests, wetlands and soils; safer settlements; livable cities; stronger communities; and a natural-resource base capable of supporting future generations. That requires our planning system to move: From measuring development to defining progress; from sectoral optimization to system optimization; from project EIA to Strategic Environmental Assessment; from isolated projects to cumulative-impact assessment; from demand-driven expansion to carrying-capacity-based planning; from remediation after damage to resilience before disaster; and ultimately from merely sustaining depleted systems towards regenerating them. Consequently, the challenge before Jammu and Kashmir policy makers and planners is larger than writing another policy or preparing another master plan. It is to rethink and redo the architecture within which all these plans are made. Dr. Balasubramaniam asks us, in effect, to reconsider what progress itself means. For Jammu and Kashmir, that may be precisely the right place to begin. Development we undoubtedly need. But the real test is whether today’s development leaves tomorrow’s Jammu and Kashmir more prosperous, more resilient and ecologically stronger than we found it. That should be our measure of progress. Javed Hussain Mir, Professor of Practice (Sustainable Development), Islamic University of Science and Technology, Awantipora, Kashmir.

Tourism generates employment and income but also generates traffic, water demand, wastewater, solid waste and land-use change.
When institutions optimize these objectives independently, individually rational projects can collectively produce irrational outcomes.
That is fundamentally a planning-architecture problem.
Nature performs infrastructure functions.
Forests moderate runoff and erosion.
Wetlands absorb and store floodwater.
Healthy watersheds protect downstream roads, settlements and reservoirs.
Healthy soils store water and sustain agricultural productivity.
Urban green systems reduce heat and improve human wellbeing.

Balasubramaniam’s call for regenerative development and the Nature-based development planning approach, therefore, converge on an important idea: Progress should leave our economic, social and ecological systems stronger not weaker.
For planning purposes, this means designing built and natural infrastructure as complementary parts of the same development system.
So, where do we start?
Start with the geography that actually connects us Government operates through districts, municipalities, departments and development authorities.
Water does not.
Floods follow topography.
Sediment moves downstream.
Forest degradation affects water flows.
Urbanization alters runoff.
Tourism pressures spill across administrative boundaries.
For the Kashmir Valley, the Jhelum River Basin provides an obvious higher-level ecological planning framework.
Snow and glaciers, upper catchment forests, springs, tributaries, agriculture, orchards, wetlands, floodplains, Srinagar and Wular are components of one interconnected hydrological system.
This does not require another bureaucracy.
It requires a nested planning architecture.
At the highest level should be J&K’s strategic economic, social and resilience objectives.

Basin and landscape planning should establish the underlying resource envelope: water availability, ecological assets, climate and disaster risks, natural infrastructure and broad carrying capacities.
Sector strategies for tourism, horticulture, agriculture, forestry, urbanization, transport, industry and energy should then operate within that framework.
These strategies should subsequently be differentiated across sub-basins, districts, towns and development-authority areas, while implementation remains with existing departments and agencies.
Strategic Environmental Assessment (SEA) should become standard planning practice Changing the architecture also requires changing our assessment tools.
Environmental Impact Assessment, or EIA, generally operates at the individual-project stage.
By then, many important strategic decisions—location, development model, scale and investment direction—may already have been made.
J&K should, therefore, introduce SEA, as standard good practice for major sector strategies, spatial plans and sub-basin development plans.
The difference is significant.
An EIA asks: What environmental impacts will this particular road create?
An SEA asks: What mobility strategy should this region pursue?
Where should new infrastructure go?
What alternatives exist?
What development will be induced by improved accessibility?
And what are the combined consequences for communities, forests, water, climate resilience and disaster risk?

Similarly, rather than assessing tourism projects one hotel at a time, an SEA of a destination or tourism strategy would examine its proposed scale and spatial pattern against water availability, waste-management capacity, mobility, ecosystem sensitivity and community needs.
Consequently, SEA moves environmental thinking upstream, where fundamental development choices are still open.
Look at cumulative impacts, not projects in isolation SEA - Cumulative Impact Assessment (CIA) are essential planning tools: A single hotel may appear acceptable.
So might another.
And another.
But fifty individually acceptable developments can collectively overwhelm a destination’s roads, water supply, sewage system, waste infrastructure, landscapes and communities.
The same applies to roads, hydropower, urban construction and industrial development.
Therefore, our planning system needs to ask not merely what each project does, but what all foreseeable development together will do to a landscape or sub-basin.
This brings carrying capacity to the center of planning: How much water is sustainably available?
How much tourism can a destination accommodate?
How much traffic can its road network absorb?
How much waste can be treated?
How much construction can occur without increasing flood risk?
How will these thresholds change under global warming?
These are not merely environmental questions.
They are questions about the sustainability of economic assets and public investment.
Geo-AI can make this practical.
We also possess capabilities that earlier generations of planners did not.

GIS, remote sensing, digital elevation models, hydrological and climate modelling, sensors and artificial intelligence can combine information on forests, wetlands, rivers, glaciers, snow, orchards, settlements, infrastructure, tourism, pollution and hazards.
A J&K Geo-AI-enabled planning platform could allow decision-makers to test alternative development scenarios before investments become locked in.
What happens to runoff and flood risk?
What additional water and energy will be required?
What traffic and waste will be generated?
Which natural assets will be lost?
Which communities benefit and which assume additional risks?
Could Nature-based Solutions reduce or complement expensive engineered infrastructure?
Technology will not replace political judgement.
But it can greatly improve the evidence upon which judgement is exercised.
From sustainability towards regeneration J&K already has part of the institutional foundation for this approach.

The Jammu and Kashmir Water Resources (Regulation and Management) Act, 2010 calls for planning on a hydrological-unit basis using multidisciplinary approaches and explicitly incorporates basin-master planning.
The opportunity is to extend this principle into the wider development-planning architecture.
Balasubramaniam’s argument adds another important dimension.
Perhaps the objective should no longer be merely to make development less damaging.

In particularly fragile landscapes, the ambition should progressively become regenerative: restoring watersheds, strengthening communities, improving soils, rebuilding ecological resilience, and making infrastructure safer while simultaneously expanding livelihoods and economic opportunities.
So, what should progress mean for J&K?
Jammu and Kashmir must seek economic growth and prosperity.
But progress in a Himalayan region should mean more than increasing physical assets and economic transactions.

It should mean higher household incomes and productive employment; resilient infrastructure; secure water supplies; healthy forests, wetlands and soils; safer settlements; livable cities; stronger communities; and a natural-resource base capable of supporting future generations.

That requires our planning system to move: From measuring development to defining progress; from sectoral optimization to system optimization; from project EIA to Strategic Environmental Assessment; from isolated projects to cumulative-impact assessment; from demand-driven expansion to carrying-capacity-based planning; from remediation after damage to resilience before disaster; and ultimately from merely sustaining depleted systems towards regenerating them.
Consequently, the challenge before Jammu and Kashmir policy makers and planners is larger than writing another policy or preparing another master plan.
It is to rethink and redo the architecture within which all these plans are made.
Dr. Balasubramaniam asks us, in effect, to reconsider what progress itself means.
For Jammu and Kashmir, that may be precisely the right place to begin.
Development we undoubtedly need.
But the real test is whether today’s development leaves tomorrow’s Jammu and Kashmir more prosperous, more resilient and ecologically stronger than we found it.
That should be our measure of progress.
Javed Hussain Mir, Professor of Practice (Sustainable Development), Islamic University of Science and Technology, Awantipora, Kashmir.

stories.headline: Kashmir’s Vanishing Green Cover: Over 6.6 lakh trees felled in 5 years
stories.title: Kashmir’s Vanishing Green Cover: Over 6.6 lakh trees felled in 5 years
stories.summary: Srinagar, Oct 8: Kashmir’s tree-felling story is far more extensive than the recent cutting of 14000 Russian poplars. Government records point to lakhs of trees being removed from riverbanks and for infrastructure projects in recent years. The larger question, which remains unasked and unanswered, is: how much green cover has Kashmir lost, and what has actually been restored? Over 5.84 lakh trees were felled along the Jhelum and its associated water channels in five years. This was as per the official Irrigation and Flood Control Department reply to an RTI. The department had identified 6,32,924 trees as encroachments, and chopped down 5,84,153. The largest number of trees, 4,79,074, were identified as encroaching between Panzinara and Banyari, and about 90,000 downstream of Sangam gauge hut at Sampora. There were more- thousands and thousands at other stretches. The felling does not end with the Jhelum. A compliance report filed by the J&K Government before the National Green Tribunal shows that 82,511 trees were felled for 154 infrastructure projects. The compensatory levies remained outstanding, and a total liability of about Rs 49.07 crore was still outstanding. Now, recently, in September, the J&K Government told the Legislative Assembly that 14,255 Russian poplar trees had been felled across seven Kashmir districts in three years. Baramulla had 9,954 of its poplars, followed by Pulwama with 1,648, Anantnag 792, Budgam 754, Srinagar 637, Ganderbal 235 and Kulgam 235. The poplar felling followed restrictions on female Russian poplars. Although the government-constituted committee examining “health issues” related to poplar trees found no established scientific link between poplar pollen and allergies or asthma, yet it assumed that the cotton-like fluff “could” carry dust, fungal spores and pollen and “cause nuisance”. Phased removal of female trees and promotion of male, cotton-free clones was recommended. Illegal logging, encroachment, unauthorised construction, conversion of land and felling of trees on community land are also contributing to loss of green cover. The scale of such loss of trees is harder to quantify; however, the massive change of land-use that Kashmir has seen over the past decade is proof in itself. While the government records trees felled for particular projects or purposes, forest diversion attracts compensatory afforestation. However, there is no readily available record that shows how many mature trees have been felled, how much ecological value was lost, how much compensation was assessed and collected. Government data states that 7.47 crore saplings have been planted under CAMPA (Compensatory Afforestation Fund Management and Planning Authority) since 2010. Over 1.06 lakh hectares have been treated through afforestation. However, compensatory afforestation has a survival of 50-60%. As of March 2024, J&K CAMPA had Rs 851.65 crore available, while Rs 727.66 crore remained unutilized. Saplings however, do not replace the value of mature trees. The question, therefore, is not merely how many trees Kashmir is cutting, but whether, apart from felling of trees, the ecological loss is being measured and compensated.
